questions.text: Fill in the option that prints the installed Python version.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 1a: python3 -V (capital V) reports the version — useful when you've installed Python on a different computer and need to check what's there.

questions.text: Python 2 is still supported in this lab and course, as long as you use python2 -V to check its version.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 1a note: as of January 1, 2020, Python 2 is no longer supported, so it isn't supported in this lab or this course. The labs are based on Python 3.8.2.

questions.text: After typing python3, what tells you that you're inside Python's interactive interpreter?
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 1b: “The three angle brackets (>>>) indicate that you are in Python's interactive interpreter.”

questions.text: How do you leave the interactive interpreter and get back to the Linux prompt?
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 3c: enter quit() to exit the interactive interpreter and return to devasc@labvm:~$.

questions.text: Match each math operation to its Python syntax.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2a, the operations table. Note that exponents use **, not ^.

questions.text: What does the interpreter show for 20/5?
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2a: 20/5 gives 4.0. The / operator always produces a float, even when the division is exact. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Following PEMDAS, what is the result of 2+3*4**2?
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2b: Python evaluates Parentheses, then Exponents, then Multiplication/Division, then Addition/Subtraction. So 4**2 = 16, then 3*16 = 48, then 2+48 = 50. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does the interactive interpreter display for each of these lines?
options: Nothing for the first line, Hello World! for the second
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 3: typing a bare string makes the interpreter echo it back in quotes ('Hello World!'), whichever quotes you used. print() outputs the text itself, without quotes.

questions.text: Which of these run the saved hello-world.py script? (Select all that apply.)
options: In VS Code, click Run > Run Without Debugging
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 4e-g: VS Code's Run Without Debugging; python3 hello-world.py in VS Code's terminal; or python3 with the full path from a terminal outside VS Code. There is no run command in the interpreter.

questions.text: Match each value to the data type name type() reports for it.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1: type(98) shows <class 'int'>, type(98.6) <class 'float'>, type("Hi!") <class 'str'> and type(True) <class 'bool'>. Integers are whole numbers, floats need a decimal value, strings are any sequence of characters, and Booleans are True or False.

questions.text: What does type(3.75) return?
options: <class 'int'> — Python drops the decimal and treats it as 3
questions.warning: Upon double checking, a number with a decimal is not treated as an integer: 3.75 is a float. Only int(3.75) truncates it to 3.
questions.explanation: Any number written with a decimal point is a float, so type(3.75) is <class 'float'>. Python never silently drops the decimal. You only get 3 if you explicitly cast it with int(3.75), which truncates. Verified by running both.

questions.text: Match each Boolean operator to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2, the Boolean operators table.

questions.text: Which of these evaluates to False?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2: 1<1 is False, because 1 isn't less than itself. 1>=1 and 1<=1 are True because the “or equal to” part matches. Verified by running them.

questions.text: What's the difference between = and ==?
options: = assigns a value to a variable; == checks whether two values are equal
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3: “The Boolean operator for determining whether two values are equal is the double equal sign (==). A single equal sign (=) is used to assign a value to a variable.”

questions.text: What does the interpreter show for the last line?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3: multiplying a string by an integer repeats it that many times, with no spaces added. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Which line prints CiscoNetworkingAcademy — with no spaces?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 4: concatenating with + adds nothing between the strings. Separating them with commas makes print() insert a space between arguments. That's why both of the lab's versions print Cisco Networking Academy. Verified by running all of them.

questions.text: What happens when this runs?
questions.context:
>>> x=3
>>> print("The value of x is " + x)
options: It prints The value of x is 3
It prints The value of x is x
It raises TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
It converts x to a string automatically and prints it
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 5a: concatenation doesn't work when joining different data types, so Python raises a TypeError instead of guessing. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Fill in the function that casts x so the concatenation works.
questions.code:
x=3
print("The value of x is " + ___(x))
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 5b: str(x) converts the integer to a string, printing The value of x is 3. Converting between data types is called type casting.

questions.text: After running print("The value of x is " + str(x)), what does type(x) return?
questions.context:
>>> x=3
>>> print("The value of x is " + str(x))
The value of x is 3
>>> type(x)
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 5b-c: str(x) only produced a string copy for that one print(). x is still an integer. To change it, you must reassign it: x=str(x). Verified by running it.

questions.text: What is stored in pi?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 5d: "{:.2f}".format(num) formats the number to 2 decimal places. format() returns text, so pi is the string '3.14', which the f-string then prints as The value of pi is 3.14. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does len(hostnames) return?
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1a: len() returns the number of items in a list — five hostnames.

questions.text: What does hostnames contain at the end?
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1b: index 0 (R1) is replaced with RTR1, then del hostnames[3] removes the fourth item, S1. Indexes start at zero. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Fill in the index that returns the last item, 'S2'.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1b: “The last item can be referenced with index [-1].”

questions.text: Fill in the command that removes an item from a list by its index.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1b: “Use the del command to remove an item from a list.”

questions.text: Which statements about creating a dictionary are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Each entry is a key/value pair, with a colon between the key and its value
It is created with square brackets [ ]
String keys and values need quotes
Entries are referenced by their sequence number, like a list
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 2a-b: braces, key/value pairs separated by a colon, quotes around strings. Unlike lists, dictionary objects are referenced by key, not by sequence number.

questions.text: How do you get R1's IP address out of this dictionary?
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 2b: reference a dictionary object by its key, in brackets. ipAddress['R1'] returns '10.1.1.1'. ipAddress[0] raises KeyError: 0, since 0 isn't a key (verified by running it).

questions.text: What does this line do?
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 2b: “Add a key/value pair by setting the new key equal to a value.” Assigning to a key that doesn't exist creates it. Reading a missing key is what raises KeyError.

questions.text: A dictionary value can be another data type such as a list, e.g. giving R3 three IP addresses.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 2c: values can be any data type, including lists and dictionaries. ipAddress["R3"]=["10.3.3.1","10.3.3.2","10.3.3.3"] gives R3 a list of addresses, and ipAddress["R3"][1] would return '10.3.3.2' (verified by running it).

questions.text: After these steps, what does Python 3.8 actually display for ipAddress?
questions.warning: Upon double checking, the keys don't come out shuffled (e.g. S1, R2, R1, R3). Since Python 3.7, dictionaries keep insertion order, so the real output is R1, R2, R3, S1.
questions.explanation: Dictionaries remember the order keys were first added (guaranteed since Python 3.7, so it holds on the lab's 3.8.2). Replacing R3's value keeps R3 in its original slot, and the new key S1 goes at the end. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What happens when a program reaches input()?
options: It skips the line if no keyboard is connected
It stops until the user types something and hits Enter
It reads the next line of a file
It waits 10 seconds, then continues with an empty string
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 1: “If the input function is called, the program will stop until the user provides input and hits the Enter key.” The optional parameter is the prompt string shown to the user.

questions.text: The user types 36. What type is age?
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 2 note: the data type for the input function is a string by default, so you must cast it, e.g. int(input(...)), before comparing it with numbers. Comparing "10" > 5 raises TypeError (verified by running it).

questions.text: What does if-vlan.py print as written?
questions.context:
nativeVLAN = 1
dataVLAN = 100
if nativeVLAN == dataVLAN:
    print("The native VLAN and the data VLAN are the same.")
else:
    print("The native VLAN and the data VLAN are different.")
options: The native VLAN and the data VLAN are the same.
The native VLAN and the data VLAN are different.
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 1b: 1 is not equal to 100, so the if condition is False and the else block runs. Step 1c then gives both variables the same value to get the “same” message.

questions.text: How many spaces does the lab say to use for each level of indentation in Python?
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 1a note: “In Python, use four spaces to indent.” VS Code does it automatically when you save. A nested block, like the print() inside an if inside a for, gets eight.

questions.text: Match each ACL number entered into if-acl.py to what it prints.
questions.context:
aclNum = int(input("What is the IPv4 ACL number? "))
if aclNum >= 1 and aclNum <= 99:
    print("This is a standard IPv4 ACL.")
elif aclNum >=100 and aclNum <= 199:
    print("This is an extended IPv4 ACL.")
else:
    print("This is not a standard or extended IPv4 ACL.")
allChoices: This is a standard IPv4 ACL.
This is an extended IPv4 ACL.
This is not a standard or extended IPv4 ACL.

pairs.match: This is a standard IPv4 ACL.
This is a standard IPv4 ACL.
This is an extended IPv4 ACL.
This is not a standard or extended IPv4 ACL.
This is not a standard or extended IPv4 ACL.

questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 2: standard is 1-99, extended is 100-199, anything else falls to else. The boundaries 99 and 100 land in different ranges because of <= and >=. Verified by running each value.

questions.text: In an if/elif/else chain, once one elif matches, Python still checks the remaining elif statements in case another also matches.
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 2: “the first one matched will be executed and none of the remaining elif statements will be checked. Nor will the else statement.”

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.context:
devices=["R1","R2","R3","S1","S2"]
for item in devices:
    if "R" in item:
        print(item)
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 3b: an if embedded in the for loop prints only the items containing the letter R. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Fill in the list method that builds the new switches list.
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 3c: append() adds each matching item to the end of the list, leaving switches as ['S1', 'S2'].

questions.text: The variable name item in for item in devices: is required — Python won't accept any other name there.
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 3a: “The variable name item is arbitrary and can be anything the programmer chooses. Often, programmers will shorten this to just the letter i.”

questions.text: When does a while loop stop?
options: After it has run exactly once
Only when its Boolean expression evaluates as False, or a break runs
When the list it is iterating through runs out of items
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 4: a while loop keeps executing as long as its Boolean expression remains true. It won't stop until that evaluates as false, which can make a program run endlessly if nothing ever makes it false. Steps 4c and 5 use break to leave the loop.

questions.text: The user enters 3. What does this script print?
questions.context:
x=input("Enter a number to count to: ")
x=int(x)
y=1
while y<=x:
    print(y)
    y=y+1
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 4a-b: y starts at 1 and is printed then incremented while y<=x. Once y reaches 4 the condition is False. Verified by running it.

questions.text: The lab says these two versions give the same output. For which input do they differ?
context:
# Version A
x=int(input("Enter a number to count to: "))
y=1
while y<=x:
    print(y)
    y=y+1

# Version B
x=int(input("Enter a number to count to: "))
y=1
while True:
    print(y)
    y=y+1
    if y>x:
        break
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 4c-d. Version A checks before printing, so for 0 it prints nothing. Version B prints first and checks afterwards, so it always prints at least 1. For 1 and 10 they match, as the lab says. Verified by running both with 0.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks so the outer loop ends when the user types q or quit.
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 5a: or makes the condition True if either word was typed, and break leaves the outer while True: loop, ending the program.

allChoices: Read the file (the default if the mode is omitted)
Write over the file, replacing its content
Append to the end of the file

pairs.match: Read the file (the default if the mode is omitted)
Write over the file, replacing its content

questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 1: the three mode parameters for open(name, [mode]). Verified that w really wipes the old content and a keeps it.

questions.text: Why does this print a blank line after every device?
questions.context:
file=open("devices.txt","r")
for item in file:
    print(item)
file.close()
options: Because devices.txt has an empty line between devices
Because each line read from the file still ends in a newline, and print() adds its own newline on top
Because open() in read mode doubles every newline
Because file.close() prints an empty line for each item
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 1c-2: each item is e.g. 'Cisco 819 Router\n', so the line's own newline plus print()'s newline makes a blank line. Verified by printing repr(item).

questions.text: Fill in the method that removes the trailing newline so the output has no blank lines.
questions.code:
file=open("devices.txt","r")
for item in file:
    item=item.___()
    print(item)
file.close()
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 2: strip() removes whitespace, including the newline, from both ends of each line.

questions.text: What does file.close() do in these scripts?
options: Releases the file from the computer's memory once you're done with it
Saves a backup copy of the file
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 1b and Step 4: after you're done with the file, close() removes it from the computer's memory. The file on disk is untouched.

questions.text: Why copy a file's content into a list such as devices?
options: Because Python can't print a file directly
So the content can be referenced and manipulated locally without impacting the original resource
Because lists are written back to the file automatically
Because open() only works when there is an empty list
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 3: programmers usually copy external content into a local variable that can be referenced and manipulated without impacting the original resource.

questions.text: Complete the Step 4 challenge script file-access-input.py.
questions.code:
file=open("devices.txt","___")
while True:
    newItem=input("Enter device name: ")
    if newItem == "exit":
        print("All done!")
        ___
    file.___(newItem + "\n")
file.close()
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 4: open in append mode a so existing devices are kept, break out of the while True: loop when the user types exit, and add each new device with file.write(newItem + "\n"). The \n keeps each device on its own line. Verified by running it.
